section_summary: This section covers Japanese cabinet developments and internal political affairs from early 1937 to early 1938, detailing the establishment, policies, and rapid downfall of General Senjuro Hayashi's non-party administration and the subsequent formation of Prince Fumimaro Konoe's coalition cabinet. It documents diplomatic appointments, notably the naming of moderate cosmopolitan Naotake Sato as Foreign Minister, and tracks the escalating impact of the outbreak of full-scale Sino-Japanese hostilities in July 1937 on domestic governance. In response to the China emergency, the Konoe administration instituted structural innovations including the Cabinet Planning Board, a ten-member advisory body of Temporary Cabinet Counselors, and the National Spiritual Mobilization campaign, while the appointment of militant big-navy spokesman Admiral Nobumasa Suetsugu as Home Minister signaled growing military dominance and intensifying anti-Western sentiment.

subfiles.about: Report on the political opposition confronting the Hirota Cabinet following the Anti-Comintern Pact and the Sian Incident.
subfiles.summary: Reviews the domestic and international criticism facing the Hirota Government in late December 1936 after premature disclosures regarding the German-Japanese Anti-Comintern Pact disrupted negotiations with the Soviet Union over a revised fisheries treaty. Although the Sian coup attempt by Chang Hsueh-liang provided a brief political respite, organized opposition consolidated across the press, the House of Peers, and major parties including the Minseito, Seiyukai, and Shakai Taishuto ahead of the forthcoming Diet session.
subfiles.title: Internal Political Affairs: The Hirota Cabinet and Party Opposition

subfiles.about: Biographical profile and political assessment of Naotake Sato upon his appointment as Minister for Foreign Affairs.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Maxwell M. Hamilton / Joseph W. Ballantine)
subfiles.summary: Reviews the diplomatic career of fifty-seven-year-old Naotake Sato, adopted son of former Ambassador Aimaro Sato, noting his extensive service in Europe and prominent work with the League of Nations in Geneva. Characterizes Sato as a cultured, cosmopolitan diplomat with liberal international attitudes who is cautious by temperament and unlikely to initiate radical shifts in Japanese foreign policy. Observes that Sato accepted the post under General Hayashi after younger diplomats, including Ambassador Hirosi Saito in Washington, declined due to expectations that the Hayashi Cabinet would be short-lived.
subfiles.title: Mr. Naotake Sato, Recently Appointed Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 2256 concerning the statement of general policies issued by General Hayashi.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Tokyo Despatch No. 2256 (filed under 894.00/701) to 894.002/324. It indexes the formal statement issued by General Senjuro Hayashi setting forth the general policies of his newly installed administration.
subfiles.title: Policies of the Hayashi Cabinet: Statement Issued by General Hayashi

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 69 regarding Naotake Sato's appointment as Foreign Minister and press commentary.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Tokyo Telegram No. 69 (filed under 894.00/700) to 894.002/325. It indexes reporting on Naotake Sato's installation as Minister for Foreign Affairs, his public record, and Japanese press reactions.
subfiles.title: Naotake Sato: Appointed Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting the installation, press conference statements, and media reaction regarding Foreign Minister Naotake Sato.
subfiles.summary: Reports that Naotake Sato was installed as Minister for Foreign Affairs after more than thirty years in the diplomatic service, primarily in Europe. In an interview with Japanese journalists, Sato emphasized the imperative for foreign policy continuity, acknowledged potential friction in reconciling his views with military colleagues, and expressed regret over his unfamiliarity with domestic politics after long residence abroad. Vernacular newspapers including the Asahi, Hochi, Nichi Nichi, and Yomiuri welcomed his appointment, highlighting his integrity, moderate liberal outlook, and potential to unify foreign policy toward China and the Soviet Union.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 69: Installation and Press Reaction to Foreign Minister Naotake Sato

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 306 regarding French diplomat René Massigli's favorable views on Sato's appointment.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Paris Telegram No. 306 (filed under 894.00/707) to 894.002/326. It indexes the diplomatic reactions of René Massigli of the French Foreign Office to the appointment of Sato as Japanese Foreign Minister.
subfiles.title: Appointment of Sato as Minister for Foreign Affairs of Japan: Views of Massigli

subfiles.about: Telegram conveying French Foreign Office official René Massigli's positive assessment of Foreign Minister Naotake Sato.
subfiles.summary: Transmits confidential comments from René Massigli of the French Foreign Office, who considered Sato's appointment a very hopeful development. Massigli described Sato as honest, straightforward, and moderate, noting information that Sato laid down his own conditions prior to accepting office and would not be a mere rubber stamp. He added that had Sato been in power, the German-Japanese Anti-Comintern agreement would not have been concluded, and expressed belief that Sato would work to attenuate its effects.
subfiles.title: Paris Telegram No. 306: Massigli's Assessment of Foreign Minister Sato

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 2257 regarding political reports on the formation of the Hayashi Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Tokyo Despatch No. 2257 (filed under 893.00 P.R./110) to 894.002/327. It indexes reports detailing the fall of the Hirota Cabinet and the formation of a new government under General Senjuro Hayashi.
subfiles.title: The Cabinet: Formation of New Cabinet

subfiles.about: Report excerpt detailing the Army's veto of General Kazunari Ugaki and the eventual appointment of General Senjuro Hayashi.
subfiles.summary: Details the cabinet crisis of late January 1937 following the resignation of the Hirota Cabinet, during which the Emperor requested liberal General Kazunari Ugaki to form a cabinet. The Army refused to nominate a War Minister on the pretext that it could not maintain military discipline under Ugaki, prompting widespread popular indignation. Following Baron Hiranuma's refusal to accept the premiership, retired General Senjuro Hayashi was selected to form the government with assured military support.
subfiles.title: Internal Political Affairs: The Cabinet Formation and Army Obstruction of General Ugaki

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 4845 from Bern regarding personal impressions of Foreign Minister Naotake Sato.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Bern Despatch No. 4845 (filed under 701.9451/14) to 894.002/328. It indexes Minister Hugh R. Wilson's diplomatic despatch evaluating the appointment of Naotake Sato as Minister for Foreign Affairs.
subfiles.title: Naotake Sato Named Minister for Foreign Affairs at Tokyo: Impression Thereof

subfiles.about: Despatch providing intimate character appraisals of Japanese diplomats Naotake Sato, Yotaro Sugimura, and Masa-aki Hotta.
subfiles.summary: Minister Wilson analyzes major diplomatic appointments, observing that three prominent disciples of the moderate Shidehara school—Naotake Sato, Yotaro Sugimura, and Masa-aki Hotta—have been elevated to key posts. Wilson recounts his close working relationship with Sato at disarmament conferences and Geneva, praising his ability to inspire affectionate confidence and emphasizing Sato's private distress over the Rome-Berlin axis and the Anti-Comintern Pact. He also provides assessments of Sugimura's dedication to the League of Nations and Hotta's regret over the collapse of naval limitation agreements.
subfiles.title: Bern Despatch No. 4845: Changes in the Japanese Diplomatic Service

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 2314 regarding the roster and initial policy statements of the Hayashi Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Tokyo Despatch No. 2314 (filed under 894.00 P.R./111) to 894.002/329. It indexes reports listing the members of General Senjuro Hayashi's cabinet installed on February 2, 1937, along with analysis of early policy announcements.
subfiles.title: Cabinet Under the Premiership of General Senjuro Hayashi: Members Listed

subfiles.about: Report excerpt detailing the ministerial lineup and early policy declarations of the Hayashi administration.
subfiles.summary: Provides the official membership list of the Hayashi Cabinet installed on February 2, 1937, noting the rapid replacement of stop-gap War Minister Kotaro Nakamura by General Gen Sugiyama on February 10. Assesses the Cabinet's initial policy announcement of February 8 as vague and nebulous, while noting that Premier Hayashi's February 15 Diet address adopted a conciliatory posture toward parliamentary parties.
subfiles.title: Internal Political Affairs: The Hayashi Cabinet Roster and Initial Policy Declarations

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 107 regarding the Hayashi Cabinet's general policy platform for the election.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Tokyo Telegram No. 107 (filed under 894.00/732) to 894.002/330. It records the outline of general policies published by the Hayashi Cabinet in anticipation of the April 30, 1937 general election.
subfiles.title: General Policies of the Cabinet: Outline Issued for General Election

subfiles.about: Telegram summarizing the eight-point general policy program promulgated by the Hayashi Cabinet ahead of the general election.
subfiles.summary: Summarizes the eight-point general policy program issued by the Hayashi Cabinet prior to the April 30 general election. The platform emphasizes educational reform clarifying national policy, parliamentary and administrative restructuring including a central air bureau, establishment of an independent national diplomatic policy, defense replenishment and general mobilization readiness, social welfare improvements, synthetic industrial expansion and raw material self-sufficiency, agricultural rehabilitation, and fiscal adjustments to curb price inflation.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 107: Eight-Point General Policy Outline of the Hayashi Cabinet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 2395 regarding proposals to establish a Japanese Planning Board.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Tokyo Despatch No. 2395 (filed under 894.00/736) to 894.002/331. It indexes analysis regarding widespread suggestions for new government planning bodies and commissions, interpreting this phenomenon as reflecting public distrust in established political machinery.
subfiles.title: Proposed Japanese Planning Board: Suggestions for New Commissions and Bureaus

subfiles.about: Telegram appraising the character and commercial orientation of Commerce Minister Shinji Yoshino in the Konoe Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Evaluates Shinji Yoshino, newly appointed Minister of Commerce and Industry in Prince Konoe's Cabinet. Grew notes that Yoshino previously served as Vice Minister and collaborated with Saburo Kurusu in negotiating the 1935 five-point memorandum with foreign oil representatives, describing him as realistic, dedicated to Japanese industrial advancement, and favorably disposed toward foreign commercial interests.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 149: Background and Views of Commerce Minister Shinji Yoshino

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 141 concerning the sudden resignation of the Hayashi Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Tokyo Telegram No. 141 (filed under 894.00/738) to 894.002/333. It indexes reporting on the resignation of the Hayashi Cabinet following a strong public statement by Prince Konoe and pressure from the political parties.
subfiles.title: Hayashi Cabinet: Resignation Following Statements by Prince Konoe

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting the en bloc resignation of the Hayashi Cabinet following public censure by Prince Konoe.
subfiles.summary: Reports that the Hayashi Cabinet resigned en bloc on the afternoon of May 31 following a coordinated drive by parliamentary parties. The decision was catalyzed by Prince Konoe's forceful statement arguing that the government should have included party leaders immediately after the election. High Japanese authorities characterized the administration's collapse as resulting from a serious error in political judgment by Premier Hayashi.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 141: Resignation of the Hayashi Cabinet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 143 regarding Prince Konoe's selection to organize a new government.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Tokyo Telegram No. 143 (filed under 894.00/739) to 894.002/334. It indexes press reports announcing the selection of Prince Fumimaro Konoe to succeed General Hayashi and form a new cabinet.
subfiles.title: Resignation of Hayashi Cabinet; Forming of New Cabinet by Prince Konoye

subfiles.about: Brief telegram confirming press reports that Prince Konoe has been chosen to form a new cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Informs the Department of State that Tokyo press reports confirm Prince Fumimaro Konoe has been selected to form a new cabinet, with further verification and political analysis to follow.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 143: Prince Konoe Commanded to Form Cabinet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 144 regarding Prince Konoe's efforts to recruit Koki Hirota into the cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Tokyo Telegram No. 144 (filed under 894.00/740) to 894.002/335. It indexes reporting on Konoe's cabinet organization and his personal attempts to persuade former Premier Hirota to assume the Foreign Ministry portfolio.
subfiles.title: Attempt of Prince Konoe to Form a New Cabinet: Persuasion of Hirota

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting Konoe's progress in forming a coalition cabinet and his overtures to Koki Hirota.
subfiles.summary: Confirms that Prince Konoe has undertaken cabinet formation with general expectations of success, seeking a coalition that includes Minseito and Seiyukai representatives while retaining the service and finance ministers. Reports that Konoe is attempting to persuade his personal friend and political advisor Koki Hirota to accept the Foreign Ministry, though Naotake Sato may remain or Konoe may temporarily assume the role if Hirota declines.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 144: Progress and Composition of the Proposed Konoe Cabinet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 148 on the investiture and composition of the Konoe Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Tokyo Telegram No. 148 (filed under 894.00/744) to 894.002/336. It indexes analysis of the selection of Konoe's cabinet members, noting the formal investiture and Okinori Kaya's acceptance of the Finance portfolio.
subfiles.title: Selection of Konoe to Form New Cabinet; Composition of Same

subfiles.about: Duplicate transmission of Telegram No. 141 detailing the circumstances behind the Hayashi Cabinet's collapse.
subfiles.summary: Provides a duplicate copy of the priority telegram reporting the resignation of General Senjuro Hayashi's cabinet on May 31. Reassesses the political maneuvers leading to the collapse, highlighting Prince Konoe's pivotal public declaration and the concerted opposition of major parliamentary parties.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 141 (Duplicate): Resignation of the Hayashi Cabinet

subfiles.about: Telegram analyzing public reception, military-industrial policies, and financial concerns surrounding the new Konoe administration.
subfiles.summary: Analyzes public and political reactions to the newly organized Konoe Cabinet, cautioning that although parliamentary parties possess destructive power, Konoe's widespread popularity justifies avoiding overly close association with them. The retention of the War and Navy ministers indicates policies favoring military rearmament and expanded industrial production capacity, while commercial circles view the appointment of Dr. Eiichi Baba to the Home Ministry with apprehension due to his unorthodox financial views and support for state control. Grew notes that while the collapse of the Hayashi administration eliminated political uncertainties, close observation is needed to see if Finance Minister Kaya can counteract inflation.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 148 (Sections 2–3): Public Reaction and Economic Implications of the Konoe Cabinet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 145 on ministerial acceptances by Hirota and Kaya in the Konoe Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Tokyo Telegram No. 145 (filed under 894.00/743) to 894.002/337. It records that Koki Hirota accepted the Foreign Affairs portfolio, Okinori Kaya accepted Finance, and the service ministers were confirmed in office.
subfiles.title: The New Cabinet: Hirota and Kaya Accept Portfolios

subfiles.about: Telegram confirming ministerial appointments of Hirota, Kaya, and the service ministers in the Konoe Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Reports immediate confirmation from the Japanese Foreign Office that Koki Hirota has agreed to head Foreign Affairs, Okinori Kaya has accepted the Finance Ministry, and the reappointments of the Ministers of War and Navy have been finalized. Completion and formal announcement of the new cabinet are expected before the close of the day.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 145: Confirmation of Hirota, Kaya, and Service Ministers in Konoe Cabinet

subfiles.about: Memorandum analyzing Prince Fumimaro Konoe's noble background, political career, and prospects as Prime Minister.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Joseph W. Ballantine)
subfiles.summary: Provides a detailed biographical and political evaluation of forty-five-year-old Prince Fumimaro Konoe, the youngest prime minister in modern Japanese history, tracing his ancient court nobility lineage and previous tenure as President of the House of Peers. Ballantine explains that Konoe was sought for the premiership due to his immense prestige and capacity to unite opposing factions following General Hayashi's inept governance. Although trained in world affairs under Prince Saionji and familiar with American perspectives from his 1934 visit, Konoe's selection represents a compromise coalition rather than a victory for liberalism.
subfiles.title: The Selection of Prince Konoye as Prime Minister of Japan

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for a Far Eastern Division memorandum regarding the composition of the Konoe Cabinet.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Joseph W. Ballantine)
subfiles.summary: Cross-references a State Department memorandum by Joseph W. Ballantine (filed under 894.00/747) to 894.002/339. It indexes an assessment of the ministerial makeup of Prince Konoe's cabinet and public reactions to his appointees.
subfiles.title: New Cabinet Under Prince Konoye: Composition and Reaction to Appointees

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 2454 regarding the fall of the Hayashi administration.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Tokyo Despatch No. 2454 (filed under 894.00/748) to 894.002/340. It catalogs diplomatic reports reviewing the events and underlying causes surrounding the fall of the Hayashi Cabinet.
subfiles.title: Fall of the Hayashi Cabinet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 2469 regarding the installation of the Konoe Cabinet and talks with Foreign Minister Hirota.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Tokyo Despatch No. 2469 (filed under 894.00/750) to 894.002/341. It notes the installation of the Konoe Cabinet on June 4, 1937, and encloses a memorandum of conversation with Foreign Minister Koki Hirota.
subfiles.title: Konoe Cabinet: Composition of Cabinet Installed June 4, 1937

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 226 on Hirota's foreign policy address and the Cabinet declaration on North China.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Tokyo Telegram No. 226 (filed under 793.94/9005) to 894.002/342. It indexes Foreign Minister Hirota's speech in the Diet and an official Cabinet declaration affirming Japanese intentions to protect nationals and secure communications between Peiping and the sea.
subfiles.title: Minister for Foreign Affairs' Address and Cabinet Statement on North China

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting Foreign Minister Hirota's Diet speech, an official Cabinet policy statement, and military preparations in North China.
subfiles.summary: Reports that Foreign Minister Hirota's foreign relations address in the Diet was cabled to Washington, while an official Cabinet statement asserted Japan had no territorial designs in North China but would safeguard communications between Peiping and the sea and protect foreign rights. The Cabinet statement was timed to encourage compliance by the Chinese 29th Army with a Japanese commander's ultimatum. Grew highlights extensive southward troop movements in Japan, observing that while technically precautionary, the situation signaled an approaching major crisis.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 226: Foreign Minister's Diet Speech and Cabinet Declaration on North China Crisis

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 2462 regarding press interpretations of the April 30, 1937 Diet election.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Tokyo Despatch No. 2462 (filed under 894.00 P.R./114) to 894.002/343. It indexes analysis of the April 30, 1937 general election results and subsequent policy statements issued by the Cabinet.
subfiles.title: The Cabinet and Political Parties: Results of the Diet Election of April 30, 1937

subfiles.about: Report excerpt detailing the electoral defeat of the Hayashi Cabinet and the political maneuvering culminating in its resignation.
subfiles.summary: Analyzes the April 30, 1937 general election, which the Japanese press interpreted as a decisive defeat for the Hayashi Cabinet and a triumph for the political parties. Despite the Cabinet's post-election declaration claiming the dissolution aimed to regenerate constitutional government, opposition from the Seiyukai, Minseito, and Shakai Taishuto intensified over Hayashi's refusal to include party ministers. The administration ultimately resigned en bloc on May 31 following a public statement by Prince Konoe criticizing the premier's intransigence, while efforts to establish a pro-government reactionary party foundered.
subfiles.title: Internal Political Affairs: The April 30 Diet Election and the Fall of the Hayashi Cabinet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 2503 transmitting the ministerial roster of the Konoe Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Tokyo Despatch No. 2503 (filed under 894.00 P.R./115) to 894.002/344. It indexes the formal ministerial roster and general overview of Prince Fumimaro Konoe's newly organized administration.
subfiles.title: The Cabinet: Gives Names of the Konoye Cabinet

subfiles.about: Comprehensive report excerpt detailing the roster, policy orientation, party dynamics, and institutional reforms of the Konoe Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Details the installation on June 4, 1937 of Prince Konoe's Cabinet, listing all ministers and analyzing Konoe's radio address pledging international and social justice. Covers financial anxieties surrounding Home Minister Baba, the appointment of Hirota as Chairman of the newly created Planning Board, and the dissolution of the anti-Hayashi party league as the Minseito and Seiyukai offered moral support. Also reviews the Army's four policy conditions accepted by the Cabinet, military cadet recruitment expansions, and Konoe's proposal to reform the House of Peers by reducing hereditary peers in favor of functional experts.
subfiles.title: Internal Political Affairs: Roster, Policies, and Structural Reforms of the Konoe Cabinet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Telegram No. 262 regarding emergency ministerial conferences on the Shanghai and North China crises.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Tokyo Telegram No. 262 (filed under 793.94/9339) to 894.002/345. It indexes reporting on night ministerial discussions and an emergency cabinet session called to address the outbreak of hostilities in Shanghai.
subfiles.title: Sino-Japanese Situation: Shanghai and North China Emergency Meetings

subfiles.about: Telegram detailing emergency cabinet decisions on Shanghai hostilities and military operations in North China.
subfiles.summary: Reports that a four-ministers meeting and an emergency cabinet session were convened to manage the crisis in Shanghai, where Japanese naval landing forces faced Chinese 88th Division troops along North Szechuan Road. The Senior Aide to the Navy Minister commended the fair and just posture of American officials compared to British and French diplomats, while indicating that Vice Admiral Hasegawa would avoid immediate vessel reinforcements to prevent further provocation. In North China, General Umezu affirmed defensive intentions, though decisive Japanese counter-attacks at Nankow and Lianghsiang demonstrated determination to enforce military settlements.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 262: Escalation at Shanghai and Military Actions in North China

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet and report excerpt regarding the shelving of domestic social and parliamentary reforms due to the North China conflict.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Tokyo Despatch No. 2524 (filed under 894.00 P.R./116) to 894.002/346, including a short excerpt text. It observes that domestic reform initiatives, such as establishing a Ministry of Health and reorganizing the House of Peers, have been shelved as the government, press, and public become consumed by the conflict in North China.
subfiles.title: Japanese Cabinet: Shelving of Domestic Reform Plans Due to North China Crisis

subfiles.about: Memorandum discussing Tokyo's despatch on the appointment of ten temporary counselors to the Japanese Cabinet.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Joseph W. Ballantine)
subfiles.summary: Reviews Tokyo Despatch No. 2630 reporting the appointment of ten Temporary Cabinet Counselors of ministerial rank to assist in managing the China emergency. Ballantine notes that the appointees represent balanced pairings of prominent conservatives (Araki, Suetsugu, Go) and progressives (Ugaki, Abo, Ikeda), with Matsuoka occupying a mixed stance. The creation of the council is seen as an effort to mobilize national support and prepare public acceptance for eventual peace terms, avoiding the violent public backlash that followed the 1905 Treaty of Portsmouth.
subfiles.title: Appointment of Ten Temporary Counselors to the Japanese Cabinet

subfiles.about: Despatch detailing Imperial Ordinance No. 593 and the appointment of ten Temporary Cabinet Counselors to advise on the China incident.
subfiles.summary: Reports the promulgation of Imperial Ordinance No. 593 establishing the post of Temporary Cabinet Counselor (rinji naikaku sangi) with ministerial standing to advise the government on the China incident without complicating the administrative structure. Grew lists the ten appointees—General Ugaki, Chuji Machida, Admiral Abo, General Araki, Admiral Suetsugu, Yonezo Maeda, Kiyoshi Akita, Yosuke Matsuoka, Baron Go, and Seihin Ikeda—noting their balanced representation across military, bureaucratic, party, and financial sectors. He explains that this broad representation aims to unite key national factions and build public consensus to accept eventual peace terms, recalling the domestic riots following the 1905 Treaty of Portsmouth.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 2630: Temporary Cabinet Counselors, Japan

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 2624 regarding the Cabinet's National Spiritual Mobilization campaign.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Tokyo Despatch No. 2624 (filed under 894.00 P.R./118) to 894.002/348. It indexes reporting on the Government's 'Spiritual Mobilization' program designed to strengthen national solidarity and discipline during the China hostilities.
subfiles.title: The Cabinet and Spiritual Mobilization Program

subfiles.about: Report excerpt detailing Masao Taki's appointment to the Planning Board and outlining the four-point National Spiritual Mobilization program.
subfiles.summary: Reports that Masao Taki was selected as President of the Planning Board following its amalgamation with the Cabinet's Bureau of Resources, and outlines the official 'Spiritual Mobilization' campaign adopted for the China conflict. The four-point program mandates: manifesting the Japanese spirit and enduring privations; strengthening public support and voluntary labor for the military; facilitating emergency economic policies through industrial cooperation, national bond subscriptions, savings, and anti-profiteering; and enforcing resource conservation.
subfiles.title: Internal Political Affairs: Masao Taki and the 'Spiritual Mobilization' Program

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 2654 reporting on cabinet counselors and rumors of Premier Konoe's potential resignation.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Tokyo Despatch No. 2654 (filed under 894.00 P.R./119) to 894.002/349. It indexes reporting on the installation of the ten cabinet counselors, rumors of Premier Konoe's resignation due to ill health, and military agitation for a chauvinistic premier and the replacement of Foreign Minister Hirota.
subfiles.title: Political Affairs: Cabinet Counselors and Rumors of Konoe's Resignation

subfiles.about: Report excerpt discussing military pressure for a hardline premier, the ten cabinet counselors, and Koichi Kido's cabinet appointment.
subfiles.summary: Details persistent rumors that Premier Konoe might step down in favor of a chauvinistic military premier such as General Araki or Admiral Suetsugu, and notes military sentiment favoring Yosuke Matsuoka to replace Foreign Minister Hirota. Reaffirms the October 15 appointment of the ten Temporary Cabinet Counselors, and reports the appointment on October 22 of Marquis Koichi Kido as Minister of Education following the resignation of Eiji Yasui, a move interpreted as strengthening the Cabinet.
subfiles.title: Internal Political Affairs: Cabinet Stability, Cabinet Counselors, and Kido's Appointment

subfiles.about: Memorandum reviewing Despatch No. 2740 on Admiral Suetsugu's appointment as Home Minister and his inflammatory Kaizo interview.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (W. R. Langdon)
subfiles.summary: Reviews Tokyo Despatch No. 2740 regarding the appointment on December 13, 1937 of Admiral Nobumasa Suetsugu as Home Minister, identifying him as the chauvinistic spokesman of the big-navy faction and embodiment of the military mind. Highlights Suetsugu's interview published in Kaizo magazine, which displayed extreme hostility toward Western, particularly British, influence in China. Notes that the British Ambassador's protests to the Foreign Office were unlikely to yield results given pervasive anti-British sentiment, and predicts Suetsugu will become a formidable figure and potential successor to Premier Konoe.
subfiles.title: Appointment as Home Minister on December 13 of Admiral Suetsugu and the Kaizo Interview

subfiles.about: Despatch analyzing Admiral Suetsugu's appointment to the Home Office, his anti-British Kaizo interview, and rising military ascendancy.
subfiles.summary: Analyzes the appointment of Admiral Nobumasa Suetsugu as Minister of Home Affairs following the death of Dr. Eiichi Baba, interpreting the move as a major shift toward open army-navy political dominance. Grew reviews Suetsugu's naval career, his resignation in protest over the London Naval Treaty, and his popularity among young radical officers involved in earlier coup attempts. The despatch examines Suetsugu's sensational interview in Kaizo magazine advocating the expulsion of white powers from East Asia, confronting British aid to Chiang Kai-shek, and declaring war on China to halt arms shipments via Hong Kong, concluding that Suetsugu is widely regarded as a likely successor to Premier Konoe.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 2740: Appointment of Admiral Nobumasa Suetsugu as Home Minister

subfiles.about: Newspaper clipping reporting international reactions to Admiral Suetsugu's interview and printing the full translation from Kaizo magazine.
subfiles.summary: Reports the widespread sensation caused in Europe and the United States by Admiral Nobumasa Suetsugu's statements in Kaizo magazine, noting French press criticism of a Pan-Asiatic Monroe Doctrine and Senator Key Pittman's call for firm resistance. The article prints the full interview conducted by Hitoshi Yamamoto, wherein Suetsugu asserts that Chiang Kai-shek will be reduced to a local warlord, outlines plans for a pro-Japanese anti-Communist regime in North China, and declares that world peace requires the liberation of colored races from white enslavement even at the risk of war with Great Britain. Suetsugu also advocates declaring war on China to cut off British arms through Hong Kong, bombing Canton, and reforming the Shanghai Municipal Council.
subfiles.title: Suetsugu's Views in Magazine Create Sensation Abroad (The Japan Advertiser)
subfiles.to: General Public / Enclosure to Despatch No. 2740

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 74 from Bangkok concerning Siamese internal politics and government reorganization under Phya Phahol.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Bangkok Despatch No. 74 (filed under 892.00 P.R./106) to Japanese file 894.002/351. It indexes reporting on Siamese internal political activities, specifically the resignation of Premier Phya Phahol, his subsequent reacceptance of the premiership, and the formation of a new state council.
subfiles.title: Siam: Internal Political Activities and Cabinet Reorganization under Phya Phahol

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 2735 regarding the resignation of Home Minister Eiichi Baba and the appointment of Admiral Suetsugu.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Tokyo Despatch No. 2735 (filed under 894.00 P.R./121) to 894.002/352. It indexes reporting that Minister of Home Affairs Dr. Eiichi Baba tendered his resignation on December 13, 1937, and Admiral Nobumasa Suetsugu was appointed to succeed him on December 15.
subfiles.title: Resignation of Home Minister Baba and Appointment of Admiral Suetsugu
